summary: Safed (Hebrew Tzfat), a town in the Galilee, became in the sixteenth century, in the generations after the expulsion of the Jews from Spain (1492), the foremost centre of Jewish mysticism and law in the world. It was home to Isaac Luria (the Ari) and his circle, including his transmitter Chaim Vital; to Moses Cordovero, the systematizer of the Zohar's Kabbalah and author of the Pardes Rimonim; to Joseph Karo, author of the Shulchan Aruch (the authoritative code of Jewish law) and of a mystical diary; and to Solomon Alkabetz, author of the Sabbath hymn Lekha Dodi. The confluence of Kabbalah, halakha, and liturgical creativity gathered there shaped later Judaism deeply.
description:
Safed (Tzfat), a town set in the hills of the Galilee in the Land of Israel, became in the sixteenth century the greatest centre of Jewish mystical and legal creativity of the post-expulsion world. In the decades after the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492 and from Portugal in 1497, Sephardi exiles and others gathered in the Ottoman Galilee, and Safed grew into a community remarkable for the concentration of scholars, kabbalists, and jurists it drew and produced. Solomon Schechter's classic essay, 'Safed in the Sixteenth Century', portrayed it as a 'city of legists and mystics', and modern scholarship (Lawrence Fine, Mordechai Pachter, and others) has studied the circle as a distinctive religious world in which mystical piety, ascetic and penitential practice, legal codification, and liturgical composition flourished together. This description follows that scholarship and the works of the Safed figures themselves, and does not adjudicate the mystical teachings it records.

The figures gathered at Safed, and the works associated with them, gave the town its lasting significance. Isaac Luria, the Ari (1534-1572), spent the last, formative years of his short life there, teaching the fellowship of disciples whose recording of his oral instruction became Lurianic Kabbalah, the reworking of the Zohar's theosophy around tzimtzum (the divine contraction), shevirat ha-kelim (the breaking of the vessels), and tikkun (cosmic repair); his teaching was transmitted above all by his disciple Chaim Vital, in the Etz Chaim and the Shemonah She'arim. Moses Cordovero (Ramak, 1522-1570), the leading systematic thinker of Safed before Luria, harmonized and ordered the theosophy of the Zohar in his Pardes Rimonim ('Orchard of Pomegranates') and Tomer Devorah, and is described in the scholarship as the systematizer of Kabbalah. Joseph Karo (1488-1575) composed at Safed the Shulchan Aruch ('the Set Table'), the code of Jewish law that became, with the glosses of Moses Isserles, the authoritative halakhic code for later Judaism; Karo was at the same time the recipient of a mystical diary, the Maggid Mesharim, in which he records a heavenly voice (a maggid) identified with the Mishnah that spoke to him. Solomon Alkabetz (c. 1500-1576), Cordovero's brother-in-law, composed the hymn Lekha Dodi ('Come, my beloved'), which greets the Sabbath as a bride and which entered the liturgy of communities across the Jewish world in the Kabbalat Shabbat service. These figures and their works are described here, not ranked or adjudicated; Karo's dual standing as both jurist and mystic is recorded as a matter of fact about the man and his writings.

The importance of Safed lies in this confluence: the same small community produced the dominant later form of Jewish mysticism (Lurianic Kabbalah), the authoritative later code of Jewish law (the Shulchan Aruch), the systematic exposition of the Zohar (Cordovero), and a body of liturgical and devotional creation (Lekha Dodi and the Kabbalat Shabbat, the customs of the tikkun and the vigil) that passed into general Jewish practice. From Safed the Lurianic Kabbalah spread across the Jewish world and shaped Sabbatianism and, later, Hasidism; the Shulchan Aruch became the framework of halakhic practice; and the Sabbath liturgy of the Safed kabbalists became the common inheritance of the tradition. The entry presents Safed on Judaism's own terms as this sixteenth-century confluence, with the scholarship and the figures' own works recorded as its sources.

period.note: The reference is to Safed's efflorescence as the centre of Jewish mysticism and law in the sixteenth century, flourishing c. 1500s in the generations after the expulsion from Spain (1492); the leading figures are active roughly from the 1520s-1530s (Cordovero, Karo, Alkabetz) through Luria's Safed period (to 1572) and Vital thereafter. Safed the town is far older and remains inhabited; the dates mark the sixteenth-century circle, not the town's existence, and c. 1500-1600 is an approximate marker for the period of its greatest creativity, not a precise span.

Lekha Dodi ('Come, my beloved'), Alkabetz's hymn greeting the Sabbath as a bride, is among the enduring liturgical creations of Safed and part of the Kabbalat Shabbat service; read line-by-line on open Sefaria. Dangling forward reference to a not-yet-created entity (a work).

Read and verified verbatim as the load-bearing text for Karo's code and its place in Safed's confluence of halakha and piety.
